quests.instruction: Rest your hand on a speaker while music plays, and you feel a buzz. Which flat part of your hand is feeling the vibrations?
quests.hint: It is the padded side of your hand, just below your fingers.
quests.explanation: Sound is made of vibrations, and your skin can feel them when you touch something that is making a loud sound.
quests.funFact: Some people who are deaf enjoy music by feeling its vibrations through their hands and bodies.

quests.instruction: A mouse squeaks, and a lion roars. Which body parts let you tell that one sound is high and the other is low?
quests.hint: They collect sound waves from the air.
quests.explanation: Your ears sense how fast a sound vibrates. Fast vibrations sound high, like a squeak, and slow ones sound low, like a roar.
quests.funFact: Young people can hear very high sounds that many adults can no longer hear.

quests.instruction: Hum a low note loudly with your hand resting on your upper body. Where do you feel a buzz?
quests.hint: Your ribs form a cage around it.
quests.explanation: When you hum a low note, the sound makes your chest vibrate, because sound travels through the body.
quests.funFact: Singers talk about a "chest voice" for low notes and a "head voice" for high ones.

quests.instruction: You sit in a room with a strong smell, but after a while you hardly notice it. Which body part has gotten used to it?
quests.hint: You use it every time you smell a flower.
quests.explanation: After a while, your nose stops reacting strongly to a smell that does not change, so you can notice new smells instead.
quests.funFact: This getting-used-to is called adaptation, and it happens with other senses too, like the feel of your clothes.

quests.instruction: Tiny hairs just inside which openings trap large bits of dust?
quests.hint: You have two, and air flows through them.
quests.explanation: Hairs just inside the nostrils catch bigger specks before they travel farther up the nose.
quests.funFact: A damp lining deeper inside makes sticky mucus that catches even smaller specks.

quests.instruction: A whiff of sunscreen suddenly makes you remember a day at the beach. Which part stores and brings back that memory?
quests.hint: It is the control center inside your head.
quests.explanation: Your nose catches the smell, but your brain connects it to memories.
quests.funFact: Smell messages travel close to the parts of the brain that handle memory and feelings, which is why smells can bring memories back so strongly.

quests.instruction: Your mouth waters when you smell warm pizza. Which part makes the extra spit?
quests.hint: It opens wide when you take a bite.
quests.explanation: Saliva is made by glands around your mouth. It makes food wet, so it is easier to taste and swallow.
quests.funFact: Saliva also washes away tiny bits of food and helps protect your teeth.

quests.instruction: You chew a bite of bread and swallow it. Which passage just behind your mouth does it travel through first?
quests.hint: It is the passage behind your mouth.
quests.explanation: Swallowed food passes through your throat and then down a tube toward your stomach.
quests.funFact: Muscles squeeze food along that tube, so you can swallow even when you are upside down.

quests.instruction: Which parts of your hand do you press gently into a peach to feel whether it is ripe?
quests.hint: They are good at feeling soft and firm.
quests.explanation: Fingers are very good at feeling firmness. A ripe peach gives a little when you press it.
quests.funFact: Fruit softens as it ripens because the material holding its cells together slowly breaks down.

quests.instruction: Which part of your body can feel a tiny grain of sand better than your back or your thighs can?
quests.hint: You use it to feel tiny details.
quests.explanation: Some skin has many more touch sensors than other skin. Fingertips have lots, so they notice tiny things.
quests.funFact: Your lips and fingertips have more touch sensors in each patch of skin than your back or thighs.

quests.instruction: On a freezing day, you shiver. Which body parts squeeze and relax very quickly to make heat?
quests.hint: They are what help you move.
quests.explanation: Shivering is a burst of tiny, quick muscle movements that make heat and warm you up.
quests.funFact: Sweating cools you down, and shivering warms you up.

quests.instruction: You run around on a hot day, and drops of sweat appear. Which part of your body releases the sweat?
quests.hint: It has tiny openings called pores.
quests.explanation: Sweat comes out of tiny openings in your skin. As it dries, it carries heat away and cools you.
quests.funFact: People are among the best sweaters in the animal kingdom, while dogs mostly cool down by panting.

quests.instruction: Some people see certain colors, like red and green, a bit differently from most others. Which body parts are involved?
quests.hint: They collect light.
quests.explanation: Color vision depends on special cells in the eyes. In people with color blindness, some of those cells work differently.
quests.funFact: Red-green color blindness is more common in boys than in girls.

quests.instruction: Lightning flashes, and a few seconds later, thunder rumbles. Which body parts notice the rumble?
quests.hint: They catch sound.
quests.explanation: Light travels much faster than sound, so you see the flash first and hear the thunder later.
quests.funFact: Counting the seconds between a flash and its thunder tells you how far away a storm is: about three seconds for every kilometer.

quests.instruction: You peel an onion, and your eyes start to water. Which parts make the tears?
quests.hint: They sit near the outer corners of your eyes.
quests.explanation: Tear glands make a salty liquid that washes your eyes and keeps them wet. Onions make them produce extra.
quests.funFact: Some tears keep your eyes moist, some wash out irritants, and some come with strong feelings.

quests.instruction: Which part of your body can be damaged by staring straight at the sun?
quests.hint: It needs light, but not that much light.
quests.explanation: The sun is so bright that staring at it can hurt the delicate inside of the eye. Ordinary sunglasses do not make it safe.
quests.funFact: You need special eclipse glasses to watch a solar eclipse safely.

quests.instruction: Which part of your body makes a sticky, yellowish wax that traps dust and dirt?
quests.hint: Cotton swabs should never be poked deep inside it.
quests.explanation: Earwax traps dust and slowly moves out on its own. Poking things into your ear can push the wax in or cause harm.
quests.funFact: Earwax also helps fight germs a little.

quests.instruction: On a freezing day, a wet tongue can stick to a cold metal pole. Which part should never touch it?
quests.hint: It is wet and soft.
quests.explanation: Moisture on your tongue freezes onto very cold metal, and pulling away can hurt. Keep your tongue inside your mouth.
quests.funFact: If it ever happens, a grown-up can pour lukewarm water on it to free it.

quests.instruction: I am tiny, I live on your tongue, and I notice sweet, salty, sour, and bitter. What am I?
quests.hint: There are thousands of us.
quests.explanation: Taste buds are clusters of tiny cells, mostly in the bumps on your tongue, that catch flavors dissolved in your saliva.
quests.funFact: Some people have more taste buds than others, so the same food can taste stronger to them.

quests.instruction: With your eyes closed, you can still touch your nose with your finger. Which part keeps track of where your arm is?
quests.hint: It gets messages from your muscles and joints.
quests.explanation: Your muscles and joints send position messages to your brain, so it always knows where your arms and legs are.
quests.funFact: This sense of knowing where your body parts are is called proprioception.

quests.instruction: A gentle breeze blows across your arm. Which tiny things on your arm bend and help you notice it?
quests.hint: They grow out of your skin.
quests.explanation: Each hair has a nerve at its base that notices when the hair moves, so even a light breeze can be felt.
quests.funFact: Even a very light touch on a single arm hair can be felt.

quests.instruction: Which part can sense a faraway mountain without anything touching it?
quests.hint: It gathers light from far away.
quests.explanation: Eyes and ears can sense things at a distance, because light and sound travel to them. Taste and touch need contact.
quests.funFact: Some stars you see tonight sent out the light you are seeing hundreds or even thousands of years ago.

quests.instruction: Which sense organ works only when food actually touches it?
quests.hint: It is inside your mouth.
quests.explanation: Taste works when bits of food dissolve in saliva and touch the taste buds on your tongue.
quests.funFact: Very cold food can taste weaker than warm food, because taste buds work best at mild temperatures.

quests.instruction: Someone is talking in the next room, around a corner you cannot see past. Which part of you can still pick up their voice?
quests.hint: Sound spreads out and bends around corners.
quests.explanation: Sound spreads out in all directions and can bend around corners, but light travels in straight lines.
quests.funFact: Sound travels about four times faster through water than through air.

quests.instruction: You stand with your back to the stove. Which part tells you the pot behind you is bubbling?
quests.hint: They work without you turning around.
quests.explanation: Bubbling makes a sound that reaches you from any direction, so you can notice it without looking.
quests.funFact: Cooks often listen to their food, because sizzling sounds tell them how hot a pan is.

quests.instruction: You wear thick earmuffs and still know a cake is baking in the oven. Which part picked up the clue?
quests.hint: It notices tiny things floating in the air.
quests.explanation: Earmuffs block sound, not smell. Your nose still picks up the sweet scent of the cake.
quests.funFact: People can tell thousands of different smells apart.

quests.instruction: You hold your nose and close your eyes, then eat a strawberry. Which part is mostly left to tell you it is sweet?
quests.hint: It is wet and sits inside your mouth.
quests.explanation: Taste buds on your tongue can sense sweetness even when your nose is blocked and your eyes are closed, though the flavor seems weaker.
quests.funFact: People like sweet tastes, probably because sweet foods such as ripe fruit give the body energy.

quests.instruction: A deaf person at a bus stop feels a big truck rumbling past through the ground. Which parts of their body feel it?
quests.hint: They stay in contact with the ground.
quests.explanation: Big vibrations travel through the ground and up into the body, where the skin on the feet can feel them.
quests.funFact: Some deaf people notice footsteps and closing doors through vibrations in the floor.

quests.instruction: You see a red apple, feel its smooth skin, and smell its sweetness. Which part puts all those messages together into one idea: apple?
quests.hint: It is the boss of your nervous system.
quests.explanation: Your senses send separate messages, and the brain blends them into one clear picture of the apple.
quests.funFact: Your brain uses about one fifth of all the energy your body makes.

quests.instruction: A person who is blind taps a white cane on the ground. Which part of their body feels the cane's vibrations?
quests.hint: They hold the cane.
quests.explanation: The cane's handle passes vibrations and bumps into the hand, so the person can feel what the tip is touching.
quests.funFact: A cane lets a person notice curbs and steps a couple of paces ahead.
